## Goals

- Distinguish true replicates from pseudoreplicates
- Simulate a randomized block design in R
- See how blocking can reduce residual variance

## Warm-up discussion

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise 1: Spot the pseudoreplication
A student measures leaf area on 40 leaves taken from a single tree
per treatment (2 trees total, one per treatment) and treats each leaf
as an independent replicate. What is the true experimental unit here?
What would you recommend instead?
:::

## Simulating a randomized complete block design

Suppose greenhouse bench position affects plant growth independent of
treatment. A randomized block design assigns each treatment once per
bench (block), so bench-to-bench variation can be separated from
treatment effects.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1)
```

```{r}
#| label: simulate-rcbd
n_blocks <- 6
treatments <- c("Control", "Low_N", "High_N")

design <- expand_grid(block = factor(1:n_blocks), treatment = treatments)

block_effect <- rnorm(n_blocks, mean = 0, sd = 3)
names(block_effect) <- levels(design$block)

design <- design |>
  mutate(
    trt_effect = case_when(
      treatment == "Control" ~ 0,
      treatment == "Low_N"   ~ 2,
      treatment == "High_N"  ~ 5
    ),
    growth = 20 + trt_effect + block_effect[as.character(block)] +
      rnorm(n(), 0, 1.5)
  )

design
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-rcbd
#| fig-cap: "Simulated growth by treatment, colored by block"
ggplot(design, aes(treatment, growth, color = block, group = block)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Compare a naive vs. blocked model

```{r}
m_naive  <- aov(growth ~ treatment, data = design)
m_blocked <- aov(growth ~ treatment + block, data = design)

summary(m_naive)
summary(m_blocked)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise 2
Compare the residual (within-group) mean square between the two
models. What happened to it once `block` was added, and why? How
does this affect your ability to detect the treatment effect?
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise 3
Re-run the simulation with `block_effect` set to have `sd = 0.5`
instead of `3`. Does blocking still help as much? What does this tell
you about when blocking is worth the added design complexity?
:::
